chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: Louis Armstrong as the idol of trumpeters
summary: Crawford says every trumpeter got something from Armstrong and recalls driving from Memphis to Chicago to hear him.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Okay now, we didn't -- what I'd like to ask you about now are some of the musicians that stood out most in your mind in terms of -- as personalities and as players, you know, like Louie Armstrong. How did you see him?

Oh, that man was one of the greatest -- I don't care who they are, trumpet players. They got something from Louie Armstrong (inaudible), that includes Dizzy Gillespie, Roy Eldridge, Jonah Jones and -- and many, many more. They got something from Pops, as we called him, and I knew him very well.
And they got something from Pops. That was their idol. Now, I don't care how fast Dizzy can get over his instrument and the rest of them. Of course, I caught that

great tribute to Roy Eldridge, 101 hours, I think, stayed up and listened to it, whatever I'd get tired I'd fall when (inaudible) falling asleep. But Jonah Jones, there's some Louie Armstrong in him, Dizzy, Roy Eldridge and just many, many more. That was their idol. I saw that man in Chicago, playing with Erskine Tate -- Carroll Dickinson Dickinson, that's the name, Carroll Dickinson at the Savoy in Chicago.

We drove all the way from Memphis to Chicago, Jimmie Lunsford Lunsford, myself and a few other fellows of the Lunsford Lunsford group to catch Louis Armstrong. He was a ball of fire. He had great personality, big, beautiful smile and playing that trumpet. I'm telling you. He was on the order of King Oliver. That was his idol, King Oliver, and he naturally was an idol of so many other modern day trumpet players and guys that came along. From my beginning I always wanted to hear Louis Armstrong, and that man without a doubt --
